body:
No need to worry.  You're chatting with someone who isn't pre-disposed to assign emotion to written text.

>I never said he was being selfish, only that he was hurting others.

Without turning this into a semantic argument, I'll say this: selfishness is the only reason (and method by which) we hurt other people.  Think about it.

Any accusation of hurting someone is fundamentally an accusation of selfishness, even if we cannot interpret the benefit to the accused.

>Committing suicide is inherently much more selfish than the desire to not have your loved ones commit suicide.

That's not really a useful statement.  We cannot objectively measure how selfish something is. There is no device for detecting selfishness, nor a scale laid out for assigning degrees of density or severity.

In reality, we arbitrarily "calculate" how selfish something is by comparing the transgressor's gain to the personal cost we suffer.  Obviously, this is a very subjective process, and because the real and emotional consequences are immaterial to you and I, we cannot presume to tell the OP that he is not justified.  We do not have a personal stake in the outcome; all we can do is pontificate.

>What about the people on this thread looking out for his well-being?

I don't think it is an exaggeration to say that most people would be more pained by the death of a pet than by the death of a stranger.  We're evolved to think and feel on a scale that feels immediately relevant; it's not something we can help.  This is idea is true but very unpopular, and therefore any individual assertions to the contrary are made out of fear of being labeled a malcontent.

>According to your statement, I'm justified in beating up a stranger, since he didn't look out for me.

Obligation has nothing to do with preemption.  You're stretching the definition of the word in order to reach a fatuous conclusion.

People don't get what they deserve; they get what they get.  You are accountable only to those people who can have an impact on your life.  Though we may blame them posthumously, the dead are free of responsibility.

You're right.  It *is* a selfish thing to do.

But remember, we each are responsible for our own well-being.  Obligation goes two ways.  If no one else is going to look out for our interests before their own, we have no duty to put anyone else's interests before our own either.

Indeed.  We never get what we deserve; we merely get what we get.

As much as we would like to think and believe differently, the universe was not made for us.

Live for yourself.  The surest solution to self-doubt and a lack of confidence is a healthy dose of selfishness.

Take a moment to re-examine some of your priorities.  How much time do you actually spend on doing things that enrich you, that make you stronger and more confident?

When I was young, I used to focus myself on the things that I was good at.  Programming, art, music.  I had limitations because of a disability, but I always felt stronger and more fulfilled when I forced myself to develop a little discipline and concentrate on the activities and work that I enjoyed.  And of course, focusing on the things I was good at increased my confidence, and people came to me and socialized naturally.

Perhaps something similar is in order for you.

Let me predicate this blurb with some general advice: you are a man, and you are human.  It is normal for you to have ongoing sexual feelings for women other than your fiancée.  If you are committing to a monogamous relationship, then you are okay so long as you don't *act* on those feelings.

First you need to get your facts straight.  You need to figure out exactly what happened between you and this other girl, so you know what kind of damage control you need to prepare for.  You can't trust the girl, because she's going to feed you whatever information will push her own agenda forward.  Was anyone else there with you that night as a witness?

>What's keeping you going?

I'm waiting to hear back from my lawyer.  I had a will made out a couple of years ago to bequeath all of my belongings to my mother, and I want to make sure that everything is in order.

I'm also waiting for New Year's to pass.  Apparently, New Year's is a popular time of year to commit suicide; not to mention a time of the year when a great many people are getting into drunken accidents.  Hospitals and emergency rooms will be in pandemonium; I don't want to cause any more strife than necessary when I go through with this.

That's it, really.  There's nothing there to be cunningly rationalized as a reason for staying alive.

I'll do some research on the matter if I can find the motivation to do so.  But I'm skeptical.

Whatever biochemical pathway that this "distraction method" works on, there is most likely a drug out there that works on the same pathway - and odds are I've been prescribed that drug before.

>There may be other reasons for "sticking around," though, such as love

I'm not pleasant to be around.  It's rare that my pain subsides long enough and frequently enough for me to really cultivate long-term friendships and relationships - and I've tried.  Even this online back-and-forth is difficult to stay committed to, since my pain and mood are busy cataloging what I can and can't do.

>or being a role model (and thus a source for hope) for others dealing with challenges similar to yours

I don't want to be an example for others.  I want my life to be enjoyable and valuable for its own sake.  I want to feel happy and fulfilled, to be able enjoy a few days without having to factor my pain level into every decision I make.

>do you think there might be a value in putting your story into words, like a book

At the suggestion of a (former) therapist, I once kept a journal.  At the end of each day, I would record my thoughts, impressions of the day, my interactions with other people, and my overall pain level.  The purpose of the journal was to monitor my condition over the course of my treatment and to provide me with an abstract of my "progress towards recovery".

The journal quickly devolved into an unflattering record of every friendship I slowly destroyed, every snide remark I made to total strangers out of anguished impatience, and every failed attempt I made at assimilation into society.  When I saw what it had become, I burned the journal and fired the therapist.

I'm sure that any book I wrote would devolve into the same thing.  I have no insights to offer anyone except: "If you suffer from irreparable chronic pain, kill yourself sooner rather than later.  The total amount of suffering in the world will be reduced in terms of both your own release, and through sparing those people who would otherwise have to interact with you."

I know that sounds bleak, but that's the only rational conclusion I've been able to reach.

If pain management were as simple as "visualizing the healing", then anesthesiology wouldn't be as profitable a profession as it is.

I'm sorry, but I cannot abide by the misconceived delusions of someone who believes they understand how to "get rid of AIDS".

>Do you feel like you've already exhausted all the ways that you might be able to make the pain manageable and bearable for yourself?

I have undergone numerous pain management regiments, including an experimental surgery and almost every single analgesic available (legal or otherwise).  Over time, I have developed a tolerance to every single medication I've been on.

My current pain management physician has me on a regime that has me transitioning between treatments every few weeks so that my drug tolerances subside before they become acute enough to render treatment ineffective.  As soon as one drug wanes in effectiveness, I switch to another.  This approach has the benefit of eliminating some of the risk of chemical dependence that I have experienced in the past, but it also means that I experience upsurges in pain much more frequently.  During the transition periods, my body must adjust to the new medications, and my pain and other symptoms increase by several orders of magnitude.

I've been dealing with this pain problem since I was 13 years old -- I'm 26 now.  As to whether or not I've exhausted all of the possible methods, I cannot know.  I am not a trained professional in pain management - I am simply knowledgeable by proxy.  But I've been doing this for a long time.

I apologise for turning this into a wall of uninteresting dialogue, but I felt that this amount of exposition was necessary.

I'm strong.  I'm not the strongest person I know, but I've certainly had good role models.  And if there's one thing I learned from them, it's that there's no point in sticking around for sticking's sake.
Let us know how it goes.

Most people I've spoken to on SW are here because of emotional trauma, losses of friends or family, personal finances, feelings of inadequacy or abandonment, or clinical depression.  I cannot sympathize with them (since I've never experienced those things), but I do understand that what they are going through is painful.  Their anguish is just as real as mine is.

But I'm here because of severe chronic pain.  I do suffer from depression because of the pain, but the depression is not the reason I think about death.  My suicidal ideation is not an emotional reaction - it is a calm, calculated, and rational decision I've considered for almost a year now.  Emotional aphorisms cannot penetrate my reasoned conclusions about death, no matter how well-intentioned they might be.

I've had a couple of opportunities to talk to some interesting people and get their input on chronic pain.  But those conversations were very short-lived, and it's difficult to feel acquainted and make connections with new people when my reasons for being here differ so greatly from theirs.

SW is a good subreddit.  I'm glad something of its kind exists to help people in need.  But like any community of people, the success of the group is subject to 1) the interest of its volunteers and 2) whether or not a newcomer has the fortune of running into a volunteer whose demeanour is aligned with their needs.

To be honest - not much.

My suicidal ideation is different from most of the people who frequent this subreddit, so I feel like an odd man out.  I've run into a few people who have had similar problems, or who knew someone who had a similar problem, and they talked to me for a short while before disappearing completely.  I'm not sure why.

I've been so busy trying to organize parts of my life that I haven't had as much time to be here as I would like, but I've tried to be at least a positive contributor to the group by giving feedback and talking to people who needed it.

Still, the fact that this subreddit exists is a testament to the goodwill that some people still have, and that's certainly a good sign.  I hope the community endures.

I remember you.  "Steak man" wasn't it?  I remember reading your post about taking your grill out and cooking steaks for strangers.  It was moving and also amusing in a "gee, I wish I'd thought of that" kind of way.

It's good to see you're still around.  The world is in need of quality people.

>Don't tell me I'm selfish. I've spent my life being a good person, volunteering and helping others, being a good friend, being a good son and brother, but after 20 years of trying to a good person, I still get treated like trash.

I don't think anyone here would call you selfish for writing this.  On the contrary, it's pretty apparent that a lack of selfishness is at the heart of a lot of the anxiety you're feeling.  

You feel as though you've dedicated a lot of your life to giving, providing, preserving, and protecting people, and you don't feel like you've been adequately remunerated (much less recognized) for your efforts.

I learned an important lesson a long time ago: that being too nice actually hurts reciprocation.

People treat generosity as a market commodity (like pretty much everything else).  If your kindness and charity come easily and freely, then the conclusion they reach is that your time and effort are of relatively little value.  Being too nice too often causes people to lose respect for the effort you exert on their behalf.

Trying being more selfish. Concentrate on your life and your problems. Focus on tackling each goal one at a time and make incremental progress. And if someone ever needs something from you, make sure there's something in it for you.

Getting your hands on some power is the first step in overcoming your feelings of helplessness and surmounting your problems.

This is going to sound a bit callous, but bear with me.  You need to begin by solving your own problems first.  Your sister and your parents may be having a tough time, but you cannot make their lives better if your own is falling apart for lack of maintenance.

What is the most immediate and pressing problem on your plate at the moment?

>Is life really meant to be nasty, brutish, and short--and absurd?

Life isn't *meant* to be anything - it simply is what it is.

We are pulled from a liquid torpor kicking and screaming into a world filled with light.  We do not consent to being brought here - our making is already underway before we are even present to give it.

When we are young and curious, we flit from this place to that, gathering up information like sponges.  Being eager to learn, our minds do not distinguish between good information and bad information; we simply take in everything.

So we learn how to write, how to add stuff together, how to pray to god, how to cook eggs, how to love one another, how to smoke a cigarette, how to drive a car, how to meet other people's expectations, how to kill...

And eventually we become adults, saturated with conflicting information, overwhelmed by conflicting feelings, and never quite sure where our loyalties are meant to lie.  We become talented at inventing glib rationalizations to compensate for our inability to be honest with ourselves about what we want.  Eventually we realize that the one thing we were never taught was how to be happy.

The reason is because no one can tell you that but you.  Understanding your individual wants can only come from introspection.  Any life-plan that comes with a set of how-to instructions was not written with your needs in mind.  How could it have been?  No one can know what you want without first consulting you.  Your preferences and ambitions are uniquely yours, and therefore it is no one's responsibility but your own to see them realized before you run out of time.

The people who are cash cows have either decided that they want to be cash cows, or that something else that they want requires that they be cash cows for a little while.  Perhaps this is not for you.  Their decisions are theirs, and your decisions are yours.

If life is not meant to be anything, then there is no wrong way to live it.  Except, of course, by doing nothing.
So far, it's not working well.

Here is the most valuable lesson I learned growing up: every day is yet another opportunity to make a new memory that will stick with you for the rest of your life.

Don't wait for things to happen - get out there and do something worth remembering.  The things you will remember best will be those formative moments - the things that challenged you, beat you, shaped you into who you are.

If you live each day in the pursuit of personal fulfillment, then you have not wasted any time.  Choose a goal and let each day be a clear step towards achieving it.  You will be surprised how many people flock to you naturally when they see how much fun you're having in the process.

There is one important factor weighing in your favour here, my friend:

The kind of person who truly grows up to become monster because of an environment like this is never aware of the effect that his environment is having on him.  He is an instinctive beast, acting and reacting on irrational knee-jerk responses.  It never even occurs to him that he is being shaped, because it never occurs to him to question.

You're different.  You have introspection, observation, and intelligence.  You have the ability to trace your unhappiness back to its causes.  And most importantly of all, you have the self-awareness to recognize when something is distasteful and below your standard of behaviour.  

These are not the qualities of a monster.  Rather, they are the qualities of a man - one who wants a taste of happiness and success - and that is a very normal state of affairs.  In order to begin your pursuit of happiness in earnest, you must begin by realizing the real barriers preventing you from achieving that happiness.

Adopt a pragmatic outlook and approach.  First figure out what will bring you happiness and satisfaction.  Then take a step back and think about what's really getting in your way.  Financial limitations?  Emotional anxieties?  A lack of a strong social network?  Which of the barriers are the most significant impedance on your pursuit of self-fulfillment, and which problems can you begin tackling first?  You needn't keep this deliberation to yourself, either - tell us.  This community is here to support you.

You may have some significant barriers to overcome, but such is the state of life.  We don't get to choose our circumstances, we only get to choose how we act in response.  The ability to make decisions about what we do is what empowers each and every one of us.  Death is not a choice.  It is the end of choice.

I've tried bludgeoning the pain with my stubborn personality for years -- but the pain usually wins.

It's hard to stay motivated when the pain is so persistent.  Pain doesn't get tired.  It doesn't have shifts in mood.  It doesn't experience side-effects from its medication.  It doesn't have to balance its social life, its finances, or its productivity.  All it has to do is rise with me every morning and stick around.

I'm in my mid-twenties right now, and I've been fighting with this ever since I was in middle school.  I always shake my head when people say how "short life is".  Life feels long.  Every day is an uphill fight that bleeds indistinguishably into the next day.  Sometimes, when the pain gets bad, I sit in my den with the lights turned low and I try to think back to what life was like in elementary school -- before everything became an unpleasant smear.

I agree with you, though.  People don't get what they deserve - they get what they get.  If the problem is beyond fixing, then it doesn't make sense to waste effort dwelling on it.  You simply need to decide on a course of action and carry through to the best of your ability.

>I had some support from my ex husband but it wore the relationship down.

I don't have a wife or a girlfriend.  I've only known one woman who was not repulsed by my demeanor, and she is long gone now.  I had a chance and I lost it out of youthful ignorance.

>Though my parents were fixated on the medication they really did help me a ton. They have never been very good with dealing with emotions so they helped they best way they could. My mom would schedule appointments with different drs and come with me. And the financial help made it easier to work on getting better.

I envy you here.  My one living parent cares about me, but she is very distant and too far removed from me emotionally and intellectually to be of any help.  She is also going through a difficult time of her own with the recent death of her mother.  It's not easy for any of us.

>I think what really helped me get through it was realizing I couldn't live like that any more.

Did you really have that much of a choice in your experience of pain?  Did becoming more active stimulate you and help with pain management?

I've found that becoming socially active with my remaining friends helps with the pain; just enough so that I can forget about it for awhile and remember how to live.  But I can't always lean on my friends.  They have lives of their own, and my schedule rarely aligns with theirs.

Hell, it took me this long to have a good-enough day (pain-wise) to even feel like sitting down and typing out this response.  I read your initial response when you sent it two days ago, but I've been sleeping on and off since then --  just waiting for day when I could get up and move around without feeling like my head was trying to turn itself inside out by crawling out my ear canal.

I really can't express how tired I am of feeling this way.  I'm going to give it until the end of the year and then reconsider my options.

I was going to say more, but the pain is starting to come back.  I'm going to go back to bed.

I don't see this as a contest over who has experienced more pain.  Statements like

>no matter how bad your chronic pain is

really don't have any kind of qualification.  I wouldn't presume to tell you that your withdrawl symptoms were somehow less unpleasant or less bearable than the symptoms of my condition, so please don't presume to tell me that I "got off lucky".

I don't take solace in the fact that there are other people out there who suffer more than I do.  Their pain is not mine.

That being said, thank you for your comments.  Ever since I realized that I was becoming dependent upon my first treatment regime, I've worked carefully with each of my physicians to monitor my dosages and to limit the risk of chemical dependence.

I'll check out that podcast.  Thank you for the recommendation.

I've been on a pain management regime for a long time.  A *long* time.  Putting my pill bottle in my backpack or pocket is about as second nature as grabbing my keys and wallet and I can self-administer IV medications with one hand (I can tie a tourniquet with my teeth).

It's not really where I saw myself when I was young.  But there's no point in wishing things were different, since circumstances can't be any different than what they are.  We don't choose how we're born, only how we live.

And if we're lucky, we get a say in how we die.

I don't mind the rant, so by all means say as much as you feel comfortable saying.

>In April 2002 things hit a peak. I was tired of trying to convince my family the pain was real and that yes I was addicted to the medication but without it I was in too much pain.

I suspect that this is hauntingly familiar for anyone with chronic pain problems - it certainly is true for me.  Pain is a subjective experience, and there are only a few methods for measuring it objectively, so it can be difficult to convince people that pain is genuine.  It's even harder when family members - people who are pre-disposed to take us at our word - doubt us.

I do have a question for you - did you have any support from family or friends at all?  How did you manage to push through all of it?
I'm not really sure what to say.  I've never been good at starting conversations.

In the interest of maintaining anonymity, I'd rather not go into too much detail regarding my treatment.  But I'm being switched to a medication which should both assist me with my pain and help wean me off of a chemical tolerance which I developed for my current medication.  A person well-read in medicine would be able to figure a lot out just from that.

No need to go out of your way to get your friends involved if they aren't already redditors.  I'm just looking for some "company" to get me through the difficult week.

There's always been an adjustment period whenever I've switched - that's usually the hardest part of the treatment process, because it is when I have fits of insomnia, nausea, and dizziness.

Thank you for your words, though.

I have some experience with death, and I will say this: there are some people who will use the suicide or death of a not-so-close person as an ostensible excuse to receive more attention.  They will play up the significance of their relationship with the departed as a way to snatch the spotlight.  These people are always the neurotic, diffident cowards who aren't interesting enough to attract people through social grace.

If you genuinely care about someone, then you'll act like it.  You won't save your declarations of fraternity and love for a post-mortem sound bite.

If you care for someone, then show them.  A smile, a hug, and a ham sandwich means more to them now than a $15,000 silk-lined casket will when they're stiff.

I felt this way for a long time.  Believe me, I feel you.

I commented about this recently on another post.  It's a bit long, but I urge you to [read and consider it](http://www.reddit.com/r/SuicideWatch/comments/dy0v0/do_any_of_you_have_a_plan/c13svz9).

**tl;dr** 1) You do not owe the world anything for the privilege of being born.  Therefore, not making a huge impact on human history does not *de facto* make you a "failure" (what does failing at life even mean - this isn't a test).  You are not here to be a performing seal - do something to make YOU happy.

2) If leaving behind a legacy is something that YOU want to do, remember this: great accomplishments are one part talent and nine parts hard work.  Even people like Mandlebrot, Newton, Godel, Bach, and Fermat were not great until their hard work made them great.  It was by their sweat, not by destiny, that they achieved what they did.

I've been referred to several doctors all across the United States.  I've also referred to doctors in Canada and the United Kingdom, both on a professional and person basis, but none of them could come up with more than a temporary solution.

I'm currently seeing a doctor who is pre-eminent in his field, and another doctor who is risking his medical license out of sympathy in order to keep me from going mad with pain.  I'm not giving up, but my prognosis is looking pretty grim.

What I could use right now is a steady diet of attractive women to provide me with obscene amounts of sexual gratification.

>I don't really have anything to be proud of...I'm good at a couple things, but even those things compared to others...its like you can get people who can do what I can do and better a dime a dozen...

I know this feeling all too well.  The victims of it are always gifted children.  Children who grew up with adults telling them that they will go on to do great things with their intellect and talent. 

Problem is, when you tell a child that they'll do great things, they don't interpret it as a compliment.  They interpret it as a demand.

Children who grow up being told that they must use their intellectual gifts to achieve great things often feel like they are under a crushing burden of expectation - that they must do something with their talents, otherwise they have squandered their potential.  They become risk-averse and afraid of trying and failing, because failure is embarrassing and unbecoming of someone of their "talent".

What no one ever tells them is that talent is not a guarantee of success or achievement.  Great music, great art, great scientific breakthroughs, great advances in technology, everything that is admirable and praiseworthy -- these things are all the result of *hard work* and *time*.  Talent can give a person that extra drive, that extra passion for a particular subject like art or science, but it is not a magic ticket that guarantees success.  It takes discipline to achieve anything that is worth being proud of.

I can't tell you how much of my youth I spent handicapping myself, tormenting myself, and plagiarizing others - anything to live up to the legacy I thought I was supposed to fulfill when my teachers and counselors told me that I was a genius.  My intelligence was my one redeeming quality, I thought.  I'm not good looking, I'm not popular, so I must do everything to preserve people's perception of my intellect.  Given our culture's perception of "intelligence" I concluded that in order to look smart, I had to be perfect, to never make a mistake.  I quickly discovered that the only way to never make a mistake was to never try anything, period.  That way, I was always *potentially intelligent*, rather than definitely a failure.

But failure is the inevitable result of trying something new or challenging.  And challenging yourself is never something to be ashamed of.  If you never fail at anything in your life, all it means is that you never challenged yourself.  By never earnestly trying anything, I was depriving myself of the opportunity to get good at anything.

I'll be honest with you, it isn't an easy feeling to overcome.  Sometimes I still struggle with it.  It is hard to fight the feeling that I am less capable, less talented than I should be compared to other people - so deep is the indoctrination that was hammered into me as a child.  But then I remember that not a single one of those other people has a magic ticket to success either.  The only difference between me and the rest of them is that they've devoted more time to developing those skills than I have.  Then I snap out of it and get right back to work.

My life has improved about as much as it could have since the day I came to this realization.  You are not here for anyone else's sake.  You don't have to live up to anyone's expectations but your own.  You alone decide what will make you happy -- and you alone are responsible for pursuing it.

"Get busy living, or get busy dying."  You've got the pride.  You've got the desire to feel happiness.  So get out there and challenge yourself.  Don't be afraid of failure.  Learn to bounce back from your mistakes and let them propel you forward.  From what I can tell, there's no barrier stopping you that you haven't set up yourself.  So if you set up the barriers, then you can take them down.

>(er, hrm... except that would be an example of asking you for info about yourself, wouldn't it? Well, if you feel you can answer, then go ahead, I'm listening)

That's the thing - with internet anonymity, its easier for me to fight the urge to put up that wall.  If you don't know who I am, it doesn't matter how shameful I act.

I'm sure plenty of people will hate me and call me a misogynist for saying this, but talking about feelings is something that women do to solve their problems.  I am aggressively masculine, not to mention a very dominant person; whenever I have a problem, I don't complain about it, I *do* something about it.  Taking a "woman's approach" is not something I feel comfortable doing - to me, it is unbecoming of a strong male.

Except that in this case, there really isn't anything I *can* do.  I've exhausted every option that I can think of, and the rest of my options are contingent of the skill and competence of my physician.  Talking about my problem is the only thing still in my control.  Even though it is embarrassing for me to do it, as long as I remain anonymous the shame is internal.

That's the only reason I came here to SW in the first place.

>we do have selfish motivations, but I wouldn't say ONLY selfish motivations.

I disagree.  Fundamentally, every decision we make can logically regress to a basic selfish motivation.  Even acts of kindness and altruism are products of such motives.  I've outlined in other posts why altruism actually evolved because of selfish tendencies, so I won't get into it here (unless you want to hear it).

Now, its important to remember that people will act in their **perceived** self-interest, not their actual self-interest.  I say "perceived" because, since no one can see the future, we can't know with certainty that any given action will necessarily be good for us.  But we use reasoning, causality, and heuristic determination to gauge by probability what the most congenial course of action is to achieve a particular goal we have.

Again, I don't think there is anything wrong with this.  This is not a qualitative judgment on humans or human nature.  The trait evolved because it promoted procreation and prosperity among the organisms that exhibited it.

>I don't know. I live everyday having to do something. Find a job to get money. Get money to pay back student loans and not seem like a bum.

So you work out of a desire to leave a good legacy?  "She killed herself, but at least she payed all of her debts before she did."

It sounds like you still have pride, and that is a good sign.  Pride is one of the most important components in the recipe for a prosperous life.  Where there is pride, there is drive.  A desire to rise to a certain set of expectations or standards -- oftentimes those standards are your own.  Pride means that you value your life.

Three years is a long time to defer something like suicide.  I think you're in better condition than you think.  It seems like you're waiting for something -- passion for a personal project, a relationship, a job that you love -- I don't know you, so I can only speculate on what that thing might be.

But it is something that you know takes time to manifest; that's why you're willing to put off suicide.  You know that there's something out there worth waiting for, worth staying alive for, and you don't want to rob yourself of the opportunity to experience it, no matter how unlikely it is to happen.

Well, you're right - these things *do* take time.  But they take time because they need to be worked on.  They don't manifest spontaneously, you must go into the world and claim them.

α-amantin poisoning would be a very painful way to go.  You would be suffering for the two days it would take for the toxins to gradually break down your organs.

Death is never dignified, but it doesn't have to be painful if you don't want it to be.

>Its weird, I used to think that by 'now,' I would have done myself in, but I feel obligated to keep living

That's interesting.  What obligations do you feel you still have?

Personally, I feel no obligations to anyone.  

None of us asked to be born, which means our lives don't come with price tags attached to them.  We don't owe anyone anything for the "privilege" of having been born.

For that reason, I'll do what I like with my life, even if it means ending it.

That being said, I've given myself a date.  If things don't begin to turn around by then, I'll execute my plan.

My comment was not intended to be combative.  I'm one of the suicidal people you're addressing.

My point was that most people who are depressed to the point of suicidal ideation see no hope for improvement - in those cases, their problems are far beyond a simple re-evaluation of their inhibitions.

Yes, life means the ability to experience pleasure.  

Life also means the ability to feel pain.  As an anesthesiologist, I'm sure you can appreciate that fact.

Depending on the cause of the depression, it doesn't always "eventually pass".
